summary: Segment Routing steers packets using a list of segments, and this works with the MPLS data plane. This document extends MPLS LSP ping and traceroute so they can test and trace paths for IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency segment identifiers.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS Ping and Traceroute can test whether a label-switched path works, but Segment Routing uses IDs that may not identify each hop in the same way. This RFC adds information so the tools can check Segment Routing prefix and adjacency IDs.

questions: how to ping a segment routing path
what is an igp adjacency segment id
how does lsp traceroute work with segment routing
how does mpls traceroute validate segment ids
subtitle: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute extensions for Segment Routing prefix and adjacency SIDs.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing sends packets using a stack of segment IDs, and an incorrect adjacency may still deliver a packet by the wrong path. Existing MPLS Ping and Traceroute need information to validate those Segment IDs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs for IPv4 prefix, IPv6 prefix, and adjacency Segment IDs. It defines how initiators include FECs and how responders validate them.
tldr.outcome: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute can validate Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency SIDs. RFC 8287 has been updated by RFC 8690 and RFC 9214.

today: RFC 8287 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8690 and RFC 9214. Read those updates with its Segment Routing Ping and Traceroute procedures.

sections.title: Testing Segment-Routed MPLS Paths
sections.content:
RFC 8029 defines echo request and reply messages for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs), used by LSP Ping and Traceroute to detect data-plane failures. Segment Routing (SR) steers a packet through a list of instructions called segments; with an MPLS data plane, the segment identifiers are labels in a label stack.

Unlike LDP or RSVP, Segment IDs are not always assigned hop by hop. An adjacency ID directs a packet to a particular neighbor over a particular link, but a misconfigured router may send it elsewhere and the packet may still reach its destination. RFC 8287 extends the existing tests to validate Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Prefix and IGP Adjacency Segment IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Segment Routing uses labels to describe a path, but a packet can sometimes reach its destination after taking the wrong link. This RFC helps Ping and Traceroute check that the segment instructions match the intended path.

sections.title: Why Ordinary Traceroute May Miss a Fault
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows a router forwarding an adjacency Segment ID to the wrong neighbor or over the wrong link. The packet may still reach its destination, especially when nodes use the same Segment Routing Global Block, even though it did not follow the expected path.

Traceroute can reveal some route deviations, but the RFC gives another case where it may not reveal that the wrong parallel link was used. The initiator therefore needs to send information that lets each responder validate the segment at the current label-stack depth.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet can arrive successfully after using the wrong link, so reachability alone does not prove that the route was correct. The new checks let responders verify the segment information they received.

sections.title: Segment ID Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The RFC adds sub-TLV types 34, 35, and 36 to Target FEC Stack, Reverse-Path Target FEC Stack, and Reply Path type-length-value (TLV) fields. They represent IPv4 IGP-Prefix, IPv6 IGP-Prefix, and IGP-Adjacency Segment IDs. A Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) describes the forwarding destination for a label.

The prefix sub-TLVs carry an IP prefix, a prefix length, an IGP protocol value, and a reserved field. The protocol value 0 allows any IGP, 1 selects OSPF, and 2 selects IS-IS. The adjacency sub-TLV carries the adjacency type, protocol, local and remote interface identifiers, and advertising and receiving node identifiers.

The RFC also adds protocol values 5 for OSPF and 6 for IS-IS to the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new sub-TLV describes the kind of segment being checked and identifies the prefix or adjacency it represents. The responder uses those details to check the segment against its local routing information.

sections.title: Building and Updating the FEC Stack
sections.content:
For Ping, the initiator must include a FEC for the destination segment and may include FECs for other imposed segments. For Traceroute, it must initially include FECs for all segments in the label stack.

If a reply includes a FEC Stack Change TLV showing that an original segment was popped, the initiator may remove the corresponding FEC from the next request, which has the next TTL. If the reply has no such TLV, it must not remove any FECs.

The node that advertised a Node Segment ID reports its pop. For an Adjacency Segment ID, the node immediately downstream of the advertiser reports the pop. The RFC recommends using Implicit Null in the relevant PHP cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The initiator includes FEC descriptions for the segments it wants to check. It removes a description from later Traceroute requests only when a reply reports that the matching segment was popped.

sections.title: How a Responder Validates a Segment ID
sections.content:
A responder checks whether a prefix Segment ID is advertised for the prefix by the IGP named in the sub-TLV. At label-stack depth zero, it also checks the relevant No-PHP flag. An unrecognized protocol value is treated as value 0, meaning any locally enabled IGP protocol may be used.

For an adjacency Segment ID, the responder checks the receiving node identifier and the advertisement in its local IGP database. For IPv4- or IPv6-based adjacency types, it also checks whether the remote interface identifier matches the interface on which the packet arrived. A failed adjacency validation returns code 35.
sections.plainLanguage: The responder compares the prefix or adjacency details in the request with what its routing protocol advertised. If an adjacency does not match the incoming interface and local routing information, the responder returns an error code.

sections.title: Traceroute TTLs with the Short Pipe Model
sections.content:
Under the Uniform Model, LSP Traceroute can traverse every hop in the Segment Routing network. Under the Short Pipe Model, the traceroute may not reach every hop because the outer label's TTL is not copied when that label is popped.

The RFC describes a technique that may be used with Short Pipe: set the TTL to 1 for the tunnel being traced, set outer labels to the maximum value, and set inner labels to zero. The initiator can trace tunnels in the stack one at a time and use the reply's return code to identify the end of a tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Short Pipe label handling can prevent Traceroute from seeing every hop. The RFC describes setting separate TTL values so the initiator can trace one tunnel in the stack at a time.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
In a network with both Segment Routing and non-Segment-Routing nodes, a responder may have no FEC mapping for the request and return code 4. A non-SR node may also fail to understand an adjacency Segment ID sub-TLV, which can prevent later nodes from reporting the expected stack change.

The RFC adds MPLS LSP Ping sub-TLVs and follows RFC 8029. It says RFC 8029's security considerations apply and that this document introduces no additional security challenges. IANA assigned the three sub-TLV types, protocol and adjacency-type values, and return code 35.
sections.plainLanguage: Some non-SR nodes cannot interpret the new adjacency information, so Traceroute may report that a later node has no mapping. The RFC relies on the security rules in the existing MPLS Ping specification.
